title: The axe in the mouth
hook: a person is born with an axe in the mouth and cuts himself with bad speech

segments.voice: Yesterday: kamma, people known by what they do, not by birth. Your line: held by its linchpin. Today, a deed done with the tongue.

Three days ago you heard the four marks of good speech. Today the Sutta Nipata shows the other side, with a story. A monk named Kokaliya comes to the Buddha with a complaint about two other monks. Not just any two: Sariputta and Moggallana, the Buddha's two chief disciples. They have bad intentions, Kokaliya says. The Buddha answers him three times with the same words. What happens next is hard to hear.
screen: `A COMPLAINT ABOUT TWO MONKS.` → `THE TWO CHIEF DISCIPLES.` → `THE SAME ANSWER, THREE TIMES.`

segments.voice: Don't say that, Kokaliya, the Buddha tells him. Have confidence in Sariputta and Moggallana; they are good. Kokaliya repeats the charge. The Buddha repeats the answer. A third time, the same. Kokaliya gets up and leaves. Then, the text says, his body breaks out in boils, small as mustard seeds at first, growing larger and larger until they burst, and he dies. The text says he is reborn in the hell called Paduma, and describes its torments at length, in the vivid, frightening terms the early texts use for the results of harmful acts. The lesson is in the verses. A person is born, they say, with an axe in the mouth, and the fool cuts himself with it when he speaks badly. Look where the blade lands. Not on Sariputta and Moggallana. On Kokaliya. Whoever praises someone who deserves blame, or blames someone who deserves praise, gathers bad luck with his own mouth. A loss at dice, the verses say, is small next to this. And notice what the Buddha did. He didn't argue. He didn't punish. He said the true thing, kindly, three times, and left the choice with Kokaliya.
screen: `DON'T SAY THAT, KOKALIYA.` · `HE REPEATS IT, AND LEAVES.` · `THE BLADE CUTS THE SPEAKER.` · `PRAISING BLAME, BLAMING PRAISE.` · then, large: `THE AXE IN THE MOUTH.`

segments.voice: Rest with your lips closed and your tongue soft, and feel how quiet it is when the axe is still. Bring to mind one person you're tempted to complain about, notice the sentence that's ready to go, and see who it would cut first. Then let it rest, unspoken, and come back to the breath at the lips.
Kuthari, an axe. In the Kokaliya Sutta, the image for harmful speech: a blade a person is born with, which cuts the speaker first.
Your line: let one word stay home. Some words do the most good unsaid. Day six hundred five.

howItsDone: Buddhist teachers often quote the axe-in-the-mouth verse when teaching right speech, and lay Buddhists who keep the five precepts include one against false speech.

fork.setup: you're the Buddha. a monk accuses your two most trusted disciples of bad intentions. what do you do?
options: expel the monk on the spot.
say, three times, don't say that; they are good.
call the two disciples to defend themselves.
fork.reveal: he simply repeats the true thing, kindly, three times. the monk walks out, and the rest of the story follows from his own words.

original.note: Pali kuthari: an axe or hatchet, the blade born in the mouth in Sn 3.10.

trapdoor: what you thought: harsh words hurt the person they're aimed at.
what it means: in the verse the axe cuts the speaker first; bad speech is self-harm.
what a scholar hears: the Kokaliya story appears both as Sn 3.10 and in the Samyutta Nikaya (SN 6.10) and the Anguttara (AN 10.89).

chat.says: Why does that old story say harsh words hurt the speaker?
options: It says the axe in the mouth cuts the one who speaks badly first.
It says harsh words only hurt the person they're aimed at.
It says Kokaliya was right, but spoke a little too loudly.
chat.meaning: In the Kokaliya story, the verses say a person is born with an axe in the mouth, and the fool cuts himself with it when he speaks badly.

Kokaliya.meaning: a monk who spoke against the two chief disciples

Sariputta.meaning: one of the Buddha's two chief disciples

Moggallana.meaning: the other of the Buddha's two chief disciples

Paduma.meaning: the hell the text names for Kokaliya's rebirth

notes: Sn 3.10 paraphrased. The hell description is summarized, not retold; confirm that's acceptable.
